title: Capable language models can outgrow the benefits of collaboration - Nature Machine Intelligence
gist: A Google Research / Google DeepMind / MIT team runs 260 compute-matched configurations across six agentic benchmarks, five coordination architectures and three LLM families (OpenAI, Google, Anthropic) and finds the mean benefit of multi-agent coordination is exactly 0.0% — with outcomes ranging from +80.8% on Finance Agent to -70.0% on PlanCraft. The single most robust predictor is the single-agent baseline: above roughly 45% single-agent success, adding agents delivers zero-to-negative gains, a rule that correctly predicts the sign of the multi-agent effect in 94% of SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench configurations. Multi-agent systems also cost 3-5x more per success in tokens and incur 58-515% reasoning-turn overhead.

insights.claim: Single-agent baseline performance is the most robust predictor of whether multi-agent coordination helps or hurts, surviving both cluster-robust inference (Probust = 0.004) and Holm-Bonferroni correction (PHolm = 0.018) while every other predictor fails at least one test.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Task difficulty relative to the base model — not orchestration cleverness — is the variable that decides whether an agent-framework purchase pays off; diligence on agent startups should start here.
insights.quote: single_agent_baseline is the only predictor that is supported by the cluster-robust analysis and the Holm–Bonferroni correction simultaneously
insights.locator: Robustness and sensitivity analysis — Multiple-comparison correction

insights.claim: Once a single agent already solves roughly 45% or more of a task set, adding agents produces zero-to-negative gains — an empirically derived capability-saturation threshold recovered from a fitted baseline-by-team-size decision rule.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: A single measurable number — your single-agent pass rate — tells you whether to buy multi-agent orchestration at all; below 45% consider it, above 45% do not.
insights.quote: baselines above approximately 45% predict zero-to-negative multi-agent gains
insights.locator: Contributions — 'Single-agent baseline as the most robust determinant'

insights.claim: The 45% threshold correctly predicted the sign of the multi-agent gain in 94% of 16 model x benchmark configurations on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench (P < 0.001 by binomial test).
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: 94% sign accuracy on the two hardest, most production-like benchmarks is what turns an academic threshold into a deployable procurement rule.
insights.quote: predicts the sign of the multi-agent gain in 94% of 16 SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench model × benchmark configurations
insights.locator: Main — 'Our analysis identifies one predictor that survives'

insights.claim: The authors explicitly downgrade their own threshold, presenting it as a practical selection rule rather than a universal scaling principle because the underlying baseline-by-team-size interaction does not survive cluster-robust correction.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: The honest framing matters: treat 45% as a heuristic that works within these six domains, not as a law that will hold on your specific workload.
insights.quote: We therefore interpret this threshold as a practical selection rule rather than a universal scaling principle.
insights.locator: Abstract

insights.claim: On SWE-bench Verified every multi-agent architecture degrades relative to a single agent (hybrid -1.3%, centralized -2.6%, decentralized -6.4%, independent -12.8% against a single-agent mean of 0.488), because most models already clear the 45% baseline.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Coding agents — the highest-revenue agentic category — sit above saturation today, which undercuts the commercial case for multi-agent coding swarms specifically.
insights.locator: Results — 'On SWE-bench Verified, all MAS architectures show slight degradation'

insights.claim: Across all six benchmarks and architectures the overall mean multi-agent improvement is exactly 0.0%, with a 95% confidence interval spanning -58.7% to +77.2% and a standard deviation of 37.5%.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: The headline number for the whole multi-agent thesis is zero expected value with huge dispersion — any vendor quoting an average uplift is selecting on the favourable tail.
insights.quote: the overall mean MAS improvement is 0.0% (95% confidence interval (CI) −58.7% to 77.2%), reflecting substantial performance heterogeneity with high variance (σ = 37.5%)
insights.locator: Results — 'Aggregating across all six benchmarks and architectures'

insights.claim: Performance swings from +80.8% (centralized multi-agent on Finance Agent) to -70.0% (independent multi-agent on PlanCraft), a 150-point spread driven entirely by architecture-task alignment rather than by model quality.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Architecture choice is worth more than model choice in this dataset — the operational lever with the largest measured effect is topology, not which frontier model you license.
insights.locator: Results — 'MAS exhibits domain-dependence with architectural variation'

insights.claim: The paper is framed as a direct rebuttal to the 'More agents is all you need' slogan and to proposed collaborative scaling laws, arguing multi-agent effectiveness depends on quantifiable trade-offs rather than team size.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: A Google-authored, Nature-published rebuttal to the agent-swarm narrative is the kind of citation that shifts enterprise buying committees away from orchestration-heavy vendors.
insights.quote: In contrast to prior claims that ‘more agents is all you need’, we find that the effectiveness of MAS depends on quantifiable trade-offs between architectural properties and task characteristics.
insights.locator: Main — 'In contrast to prior claims'

insights.claim: Prior multi-agent evaluations were conducted predominantly on non-agentic static benchmarks such as HumanEval, where teams show monotonic improvement with team size (89% with five agents) — scaling behaviour that does not transfer to tasks requiring sustained environmental interaction.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Explains why the published multi-agent literature has been systematically optimistic — the benchmark choice, not the method, generated the result.
insights.quote: MAS evaluations have been conducted predominantly on non-agentic tasks, potentially providing misleading guidance about when collaboration provides value
insights.locator: Main — 'These characteristics differentiate tasks'

insights.claim: Sequential interdependence rather than raw task complexity determines whether coordination works: Finance Agent (domain complexity D = 0.41) gains +80.8% while PlanCraft (D = 0.42) loses 70%, despite nearly identical complexity scores.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: The screening question for any agentic workflow is whether subtasks can run in parallel, not how hard the task is — a cheap, checkable test before committing to orchestration.
insights.quote: This suggests that sequential interdependence, rather than complexity alone, determines coordination viability.
insights.locator: Results — 'Task decomposability, not complexity alone'

insights.claim: Under fixed compute budgets, coordination fails in sequential domains because intra-agent reasoning for constraint verification and state tracking consumes most available tokens before any interagent communication can occur.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: The failure mechanism is budget starvation, so raising per-agent token budgets — not changing topology — is the intervention to test first in sequential workflows.
insights.locator: Results — 'The mechanism operates through fixed computational budgets'

insights.claim: Execution traces show centralized multi-agent systems inventing redundant subtasks on simple sequential jobs — one agent looking up a recipe that is instantly retrievable, another checking inventory that is already visible to all — burning token budget on coordination instead of reasoning.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: A concrete, recognizable failure pattern that operators can audit for in their own agent traces before the token bill arrives.
insights.quote: Agent 1: research recipe (redundant, since lookup is instantaneous)
insights.locator: Results — 'By contrast, centralized MAS decompose inherently sequential tasks'

insights.claim: Information gain from coordination correlates strongly with multi-agent benefit in structured domains (Finance Agent r = 0.71, P < 0.001) but is statistically absent in sequential and open-world ones (PlanCraft r = 0.18, P = 0.22).
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Measuring whether agents actually exchange new information is a diagnostic that predicts payoff before you scale a deployment.
insights.locator: Results — 'Information gain is associated with MAS benefit in low-complexity domains'

insights.claim: Financial analysis is the standout beneficiary of multi-agent coordination because revenue, cost and market factors decompose into independently researchable streams — centralized reaches +80.8%, decentralized +74.5% and hybrid +73.1% over the single-agent baseline of 0.349.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Financial research workflows are the clearest identified product-market fit for multi-agent systems — a targeting signal for anyone building or buying in that vertical.
insights.quote: The task’s natural decomposability (revenue, cost and market factors can be analysed independently) aligns with the coordination structure, yielding +80.8% improvement.
insights.locator: Results — 'Conversely, Finance Agent trajectories show when coordination can help'

insights.claim: Trace-level error amplification ranks the four multi-agent topologies consistently — independent 17.2x, decentralized 7.8x, hybrid 5.1x, centralized 4.4x — against a single-agent reference of 1.0x.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: A clean ordering that says: if you must go multi-agent, put a verifying orchestrator in the loop — the 4x difference between centralized and independent is the value of that bottleneck.
insights.locator: Results — 'Error amplification varies by architecture'

insights.claim: Baseline-scaled error amplification survives cluster-robust inference (Probust = 0.030): architectures without centralized verification propagate errors more as baseline task difficulty grows.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: The harder the task, the more a verification bottleneck is worth — the opposite of the intuition that hard tasks need more parallel exploration.
insights.quote: architectures without centralized verification propagate errors more as baseline difficulty grows
insights.locator: Main — 'The cluster-robust mechanistic effect is baseline-scaled error amplification'

insights.claim: Architectures with a verification step achieve 22.7% average factual error reduction (95% CI 20.1% to 25.3%, peaking at 31.4% on Finance Agent), while independent multi-agent shows no correction at all and amplifies errors by 4.6%.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Quantifies exactly what a verifier buys you — roughly a quarter of factual errors — which is the number to weigh against its coordination cost.
insights.locator: Results — 'Error absorption mechanisms'

insights.claim: Coordination failure is a failure mode that exists only in multi-agent systems and scales with protocol complexity: 0% for independent, 1.8% centralized, 3.2% decentralized and 12.4% for hybrid, where protocol complexity exceeds robust implementation.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Hybrid — the most 'sophisticated' architecture — generates a 12.4% failure class that simply does not exist in simpler designs; complexity here is a liability, not a feature.
insights.quote: hybrid: 12.4% (protocol complexity exceeds robust implementation)
insights.locator: Results — 'Error taxonomy reveals architecture-specific failure modes'

insights.claim: Redundancy between agents has an optimum rather than a monotone benefit: redundancy above 0.50 correlates negatively with success (r = -0.136, P = 0.004), with the best balance at roughly R = 0.41.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: There is a measurable sweet spot for agent overlap — too much agreement is as damaging as too little, giving a tunable knob for deployed systems.
insights.quote: implying an emergent diversity–efficiency trade-off in which collective capability peaks when message overlap balances shared grounding with informational diversity
insights.locator: Results — 'The correction mechanism is revealed through token-overlap analysis'

themes.theme: The coordination tax in tokens and dollars

insights.claim: Single-agent systems deliver 67.7 successes per 1,000 tokens versus 23.9 for decentralized, 21.5 for centralized and 13.6 for hybrid multi-agent — a 2.8x to 5.0x efficiency penalty for coordination.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Directly sizes the inference-cost multiplier of agent swarms — a 5x token bill for zero average accuracy gain is the core economic indictment of the category.
insights.quote: SAS achieves 67.7 successes/1,000 tokens. Centralized drops to 21.5 (3.1× worse), decentralized to 23.9 (2.8× worse) and hybrid to 13.6 (5.0× worse).
insights.locator: Results — 'Economic efficiency and family-specific cost–benefit trade-offs'

insights.claim: Multi-agent architectures consume 58% (independent), 263% (decentralized), 285% (centralized) and 515% (hybrid) more reasoning turns than a single agent under matched per-system compute ceilings — 1.6x to 6.2x more turns.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Reasoning-turn overhead translates directly into latency and per-request cost — the operational metrics that determine whether agentic products can be priced.
insights.locator: Results — 'Overhead shows a directional interaction with tool count'

insights.claim: Spending more on coordination stops buying accuracy: hybrid systems at 515% overhead and 44.3 turns achieve 47.7% success, statistically indistinguishable from centralized at 285% overhead and 27.7 turns (46.3%, t(70) = 0.31, P = 0.755).
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Sharp diminishing returns above roughly 300% overhead means there is a hard ceiling on what orchestration spend can deliver — useful for capping agent-infrastructure budgets.
insights.locator: Results — 'Message density shows a weak descriptive trend'

insights.claim: Marginal dollar cost per 1% success gain differs threefold by vendor: OpenAI hybrid runs about US$0.008, Google about US$0.012 and Anthropic hybrid about US$0.024, reflecting Anthropic's higher coordination cost.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: A rare published per-vendor cost-of-quality comparison for agentic workloads — the kind of number that drives model-routing decisions in production stacks.
insights.locator: Results — 'Economic efficiency and family-specific cost–benefit trade-offs'

insights.claim: The authors identify the token-centric communication paradigm itself as the economic barrier — agents must serialize reasoning into natural-language tokens — and name latent-space reasoning and direct activation sharing as the routes that could break the cost floor.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Flags the specific research direction whose success would invalidate this paper's economics — the leading indicator to watch if you are long multi-agent infrastructure.
insights.quote: Emerging approaches such as latent-space reasoning or direct activation sharing between models could circumvent this bottleneck, potentially altering the scaling dynamics we observe
insights.locator: Discussion — 'The economic viability of multi-agent scaling'

themes.theme: Team size hits a hard ceiling

insights.claim: Total reasoning turns grow super-linearly with agent count following T = 2.72 x (n+0.5)^1.724 (R2 = 0.974, 95% CI on the exponent 1.685-1.763), an agentic scaling regime distinct from neural network parameter scaling where Kaplan et al. report an exponent of 0.76.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Agent count scales cost worse than model size does — the exact opposite of the assumption underlying 'just add more agents' product roadmaps.
insights.quote: The super-linear exponent (1.724 > 1) reflects quadratic message complexity (all-to-all potential communication) tempered by practical bandwidth limits, defining an agentic scaling regime distinct from neural network parameter scaling
insights.locator: Results — 'Turn count follows power-law scaling with number of agents'

insights.claim: Under fixed compute budgets per-agent reasoning capacity becomes prohibitively thin beyond three to four agents, producing an observed resource ceiling where communication cost dominates reasoning capability.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Sets a concrete design ceiling — teams beyond four agents are a cost trap absent a budget increase, which caps how far the swarm narrative can run.
insights.quote: beyond three to four agents, per-agent reasoning quality degrades sharply
insights.locator: Results — 'Cross-domain generalization of coordination rankings'

insights.claim: Extrapolating the fitted power law gives approximately 69 reasoning turns at six agents and 157 at ten agents, 9.5x to 21.8x the single-agent baseline of 7.2 turns.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Quantifies the blowup for the ten-agent configurations vendors demo — a 20x turn count is a latency and cost profile most production systems cannot absorb.
insights.locator: Results — 'Cross-domain generalization of coordination rankings'

insights.claim: Optimal team size is model-dependent rather than universal: Gemini-2.0 Flash shows a clear optimum at seven agents before degrading, while the more capable Gemini-2.5 Pro peaks earlier despite a higher single-agent baseline.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Stronger models saturate sooner — so every frontier model release mechanically shrinks the window where multi-agent coordination adds value.
insights.locator: Fig. 3 caption — 'Number of agents scaling reveals model-dependent coordination limits'

insights.claim: Mixing models of different capability does not escape the saturation ceiling: across 13 heterogeneous configurations on BrowseComp-Plus, centralized heterogeneous teams underperformed their strong-model homogeneous counterparts by a mean of 12.6 percentage points.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Kills the popular 'cheap models plus one smart orchestrator' cost-optimization pattern — mixing made things worse, not cheaper-and-equal.
insights.quote: finds no evidence that model mixing bypasses the capability-saturation threshold
insights.locator: Discussion — 'Although we explore capability heterogeneity'

insights.claim: No LLM family is consistently best across benchmarks: OpenAI shows the strongest hybrid gains on structured tasks (52% versus 39% single-agent on finance), Anthropic the most stable centralized performance (mean 43%, s.d. 2.3%, lowest variance) and Google the most consistent cross-architecture efficiency (under 5% spread across topologies).
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Each frontier lab has a distinct coordination signature, which argues for multi-vendor routing by architecture type rather than single-vendor standardization.
insights.quote: OpenAI models show the strongest hybrid gains on structured tasks (finance: 52% success hybrid versus 39% SAS; WorkBench: 56% hybrid versus 42% SAS).
insights.locator: Results — 'Family-specific cost–performance patterns'

insights.claim: Static intelligence-index composites correlate only moderately (r = 0.45) with actual agentic performance, and the authors recommend replacing them with an agentic capability index defined as a model's mean single-agent performance across benchmarks, which lifts cross-validated R2 from 0.373 to 0.413.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Published leaderboard scores are a weak proxy for how a model performs as an agent — a direct warning against selecting models for agentic products on benchmark composites.
insights.quote: consistent with the concern that static benchmark composites may diverge from dynamic agentic performance
insights.locator: Robustness and sensitivity analysis — Capability metric sensitivity

insights.claim: The tested model roster spans GPT-5-nano, GPT-5-mini and GPT-5; Gemini-2.0 Flash, Gemini-2.5 Flash and Gemini-2.5 Pro; and Claude Sonnet 3.7, Claude Sonnet 4 and Claude Sonnet 4.5, over an intelligence index range of 42 to 71.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: The findings rest on current frontier models, not legacy ones, so the saturation conclusion applies to what is deployed today rather than to a superseded generation.
insights.locator: Methods — 'LLMs and intelligence scaling'

insights.claim: Capability scaling within the tested range is linear rather than accelerating — the quadratic intelligence term is flat (naive P = 0.977) — and even the linear effect fails cluster-robust inference (Probust = 0.059).
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: No evidence of a capability inflection inside the current frontier band, which argues against betting on emergent multi-agent behaviour appearing at the next model tier.
insights.locator: Results — 'Intelligence shows a directional OLS pattern'

themes.theme: Limits of inference and study provenance

insights.claim: The fitted 20-parameter regression selects the best-performing architecture in 87% of held-out within-domain configurations, versus 20% for random choice and 54% for capability-only models.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Turns architecture choice from a heuristic into a measurable decision with a stated hit rate — the closest thing yet to a procurement model for agent topology.
insights.quote: this rule achieves 87% correct architecture selection within the tested domains, substantially exceeding random choice (20%) or capability-only models (54%)
insights.locator: Results — 'The fitted model enables quantitative architecture selection'

insights.claim: Leave-one-dataset-out cross-validation yields R2 = -2.09, meaning absolute performance cannot be predicted on an unseen task domain — only relative architecture rankings transfer.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: The framework tells you which architecture to pick, never how well it will do on your novel workload — a hard limit on how far these results can be resold as forecasts.
insights.quote: LODO cross-validation yields negative R2 (−2.09), confirming that predicting absolute success rates on an unseen domain is not feasible without domain-specific parameters.
insights.locator: Discussion — 'Our regression analysis clusters observations'

insights.claim: Three widely assumed effects — a tool-coordination trade-off, a linear capability-to-performance relationship and a baseline-by-team-size interaction — are directionally consistent across all six benchmarks but fail cluster-robust correction and are reported only as descriptive patterns.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Marks the boundary between what this study actually established and what it merely suggests — the discipline to copy when reading competing agent-benchmark claims.
insights.locator: Contributions — 'Descriptive coordination patterns and limits of inference'

insights.claim: Tool-heavy environments amplify the coordination tax: coordination efficiency falls from 0.466 for a single agent to 0.074 for hybrid on the 16-tool WorkBench benchmark, a 2-6x efficiency penalty, while simple tasks with four or fewer tools show negligible effects.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Enterprise agents are tool-rich by definition, so this is the regime where multi-agent designs are most likely to fail in real deployments.
insights.locator: Results — 'Efficiency tools interaction as a directional pattern'

insights.claim: The study's authority rests on a controlled design that holds task prompts, tool interfaces and per-system compute ceilings constant across 260 configurations, varying only coordination structure and model capability — the confound that invalidated earlier multi-agent comparisons.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: This is the methodological bar competing agent-framework benchmarks now have to clear; results from uncontrolled comparisons should be discounted.
insights.quote: existing MAS evaluations compare architectures using different prompts, tools or computational budgets, conflating architectural effects with implementation choices and precluding clean causal attribution
insights.locator: Main — 'Two issues make controlled MAS evaluation difficult'

insights.claim: The study comes out of Google Research (Seattle), Google DeepMind and MIT, with the competing-interests statement disclosing that most senior authors are Alphabet Inc. employees and/or Alphabet stockholders.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: A major model vendor publishing evidence that limits demand for agent-orchestration layers is a strategically notable position — it favours strong single models, which is Google's own product.
insights.quote: are employees of Alphabet Inc. (Google LLC) and/or own Alphabet stock as part of their standard compensation package
insights.locator: Competing interests

insights.claim: The full experimental framework — all five coordination architectures, prompt templates, configuration files, analysis scripts and sanitized execution traces — is released publicly on GitHub at ybkim95/agent-scaling with a Zenodo DOI, making the 45% rule independently testable.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Open code plus open traces means the threshold can be re-derived on a firm's own workload — a practical due-diligence tool rather than just a citation.
insights.locator: Code availability

insights.claim: Claude Sonnet 3.7 was deprecated by Anthropic in February 2026 and had to be dropped from the SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench arms, reducing those benchmarks to eight models each.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Model deprecation actively breaks reproducibility of agentic research mid-study — a structural fragility for anyone building long-lived evaluation infrastructure on hosted APIs.
insights.quote: Claude Sonnet 3.7 was deprecated by Anthropic in February 2026 and is therefore unavailable for SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench.
insights.locator: Methods — 'LLMs and intelligence scaling'

insights.claim: The two most production-relevant benchmarks, SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench, were run on only 20-instance subsets because of the cost of Docker-based evaluation, giving bootstrap 95% confidence intervals of roughly plus or minus 20 percentage points per cell.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: The strongest headline claim rests on the thinnest data — treat the SWE-bench degradation figures as an aggregate trend, not as per-model evidence.
insights.quote: Bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (10,000 resamples) yield typical widths of ±20 pp per cell.
insights.locator: Discussion — 'Our analysis spans six agentic benchmarks'
